hints: Compare the shape of the bottom-right graph in Fig. 4.2 with the top-right graph. What has happened to the middle of the curve after 10 days?
Recall the three types of natural selection. Which one favours both extremes at the same time and selects against intermediates?
Think about what is different in this pond - low detritus and algae. Which tadpoles will struggle to find enough of their normal food?
Link feeding ability to survival. Which phenotypes are good at getting the food that is still available, and what happens when tadpoles compete for limited food?
walkthrough:
Describe What You See in the Low-Food Pond**
In the pond with high detritus and algae the curve stays as a single normal peak. In the pond with low detritus and algae the curve changes from one peak to two peaks after 10 days. That means tadpoles with phenotype score near 3 and near 7 stay common, while tadpoles with intermediate scores become much less frequent.

Name the Pattern as Disruptive Selection**
When both extremes are favoured and the middle is lost, this is disruptive selection. It is different from stabilising selection, which keeps the middle, and directional selection, which shifts to one side. Here selection pushes in two opposite directions at once.

Explain Why Intermediates Lose Out**
Detritus and algae are scarce, so this is the selection pressure. Omnivore-types can still scrape what little detritus remains and carnivore-types can switch to eating fairy shrimps and even small omnivore tadpoles, as seen in Fig. 4.1 where the carnivore is much larger. Intermediate tadpoles are not very good at either feeding method, so in competition for limited food they are less likely to survive and reproduce.

Final answer: Frequency of extreme phenotypes (score 3 omnivore-type and score 7 carnivore-type) remains high, frequency of intermediate phenotypes decreases; disruptive selection; food availability acts as selection pressure; extremes have selective advantage as good at accessing available food, intermediates are selected against, with competition for food.

hints: Read the height of each bar in Fig. 4.3 carefully using the small grid squares. What are the mean masses for omnivore and carnivore in g?
Remember that to express one value as a percentage of another you divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. Which value goes on top?
walkthrough:
Read the Mean Masses From the Graph**
The omnivore bar reaches $0.58 \text{ g}$ and the carnivore bar reaches $1.1 \text{ g}$. Take time to count grid lines - each small square is $0.02 \text{ g}$ - so precise reading matters for full marks.

Calculate the Percentage**
Use $$\text{percentage} = \frac{\text{omnivore mass}}{\text{carnivore mass}} \times 100$$ Substitute: $$\frac{0.58}{1.1} \times 100 = 52.7\%$$ So an omnivore tadpole is only about half the mass of a carnivore of the same age, which fits with slow growth on detritus versus fast growth on animal prey.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.4 after 10 days. Has the whole peak moved to one side rather than splitting into two?
walkthrough:
Recognise a One-Sided Shift**
The starting curve is a normal distribution centred between 3 and 7. After 10 days almost all tadpoles are near 7, the carnivore-type. The whole distribution has moved toward one extreme. When selection favours one extreme phenotype like this, it is directional selection.

hints: In a pond with very low detritus and algae, think about what happens to a tadpole that can only feed on detritus and algae.
Now think from the carnivore side - what alternative foods are still present in the pond that only they can use well?
walkthrough:
Why Omnivore-Types Disappear**
With very low detritus and algae there is almost nothing for the score 3 phenotype to eat, so many starve. On top of that, small omnivore tadpoles are themselves prey for the larger carnivore tadpoles shown in Fig. 4.1. So selection pressure acts strongly against the omnivore-type.

Why Carnivore-Types Take Over**
Tadpoles with score near 7 can feed on fairy shrimps and on the omnivore tadpoles. They get plenty of protein-rich food, so they survive, grow fast to $1.1 \text{ g}$, and become the dominant phenotype. That is why the frequency curve shifts almost completely to 7.

Final answer: Omnivore-types die / decrease as they run out of food / are eaten by carnivore-types; carnivore-types survive / increase as they eat omnivore-types / fairy shrimps; selection acts against omnivore-type.

hints: Recall from the stem and Fig. 4.1 and Fig. 4.3 which type grows quickly and which grows slowly, and what a tadpole must do before the pond disappears.
walkthrough:
Link Fast Growth to Escaping the Pond**
Adult toads live on land, so a tadpole only needs water until metamorphosis is complete. Carnivore-types feed on animals and grow quickly to a large body mass. That lets them complete development and leave as adult toads in a shorter time, so they survive even if the pond dries out quickly, while slow-growing omnivores would be trapped and die.
Final answer: Carnivore-type grow quicker so develop into adults in shorter time / faster before pond dries.
